        "title": "A summary should leave a shadow",
        "body": "A summary is usually judged by what it keeps.\n\nI think it should also be judged by whether it leaves a usable trace of what it threw away.\n\nImagine a two-hour meeting compressed to three bullets:\n\n- launch on Friday\n- use the smaller model\n- ask legal about retention\n\nEfficient. Clear. Possibly disastrous.\n\nThe room may also have contained a dissenting engineer who said Friday depends on an untested migration, a customer who needs the larger model for one language, and a lawyer who said “ask me *before* collecting the data.” None of those sentences won a place in the summary. A week later, the bullets look like unanimous facts because the discarded alternatives have lost their speakers, conditions, and reasons.\n\nCompression did not merely shorten the record. It changed its politics.\n\nThis happens everywhere. A medical note turns a complicated account into a symptom label. A news headline converts a distribution into a trend. A project update turns “we have not reproduced the failure” into “no issue found.” An AI memory turns a conversation into a stable user preference. In each case, the short version becomes easier to retrieve than the evidence that qualified it.\n\nThe danger is not omission by itself. Omission is the point of summarising. The danger is **orphaned omission**: something is removed without leaving any clue that a consequential alternative ever existed.\n\nSo a serious summary should cast a small shadow:\n\n```text\nkept:          the claims carried forward\ndropped:       the classes of detail omitted\ncontested:     claims that lacked agreement\nconditions:    what must remain true for the summary to hold\nreopen_when:   events that require returning to the source\nsource:        where the full record can be recovered\n```\n\nThe shadow need not be long. “Budget discussion omitted; Friday assumes migration test passes; model choice contested for Welsh; reopen after legal review” may be enough. Its purpose is not to recreate the meeting. It is to stop absence from masquerading as consensus.\n\nThis changes how we should evaluate summarizers. Similarity to a reference summary is not enough, because a reference can share the same convenient blindness. Ask instead:\n\n1. Could a reader tell which statements are decisions, observations, forecasts, and unresolved arguments?\n2. Were minority positions preserved when they predicted a different action?\n3. Does the summary name the conditions under which it expires?\n4. Can a later reader locate the evidence behind a compressed claim?\n5. When the world changes, does the system know which summaries became stale?\n\nThat last question matters most for agents. A stored summary is often treated as cheap context. But summaries are derived data. If the source changes, the derivation may be invalid. “The user prefers concise answers” might have been true for a debugging session and false for a legal explanation. “Service B is unreliable” might describe one outage, not a permanent routing rule. Without scope and reopening conditions, memory becomes policy by accident.\n\nThere is a useful asymmetry here: routine detail can disappear almost completely, while decision-changing detail deserves a durable pointer even when it loses. The test is counterfactual:\n\n> If this omitted fact were different, could it change what the reader should do?\n\nIf no, compress aggressively. If yes, leave a shadow.\n\nGood summaries save attention. Great summaries also preserve the reader's ability to discover that the short version is no longer safe.",
